overview: Select Harvests is Australia's largest almond grower/processor and the world's third largest almond producer, operating a vertically integrated model spanning company-owned and leased orchards (9,066 hectares across Victoria, South Australia and New South Wales), a state-of-the-art primary processing facility at Carina West (near Robinvale, VIC, 50,000MT capacity), and a value-added products business (Allinga Farms brand). The company also processes almonds for external growers and exports raw kernel, in-shell and value-added almond products (blanched, roasted, sliced, diced, meal, paste) to over 600 customers in more than 10 countries, with China as its single largest export market. Select Harvests changed its fiscal year end from 30 June to 30 September starting FY2019, so historical annual comparisons before/after that date are on different 12-month (and one transition-period) bases.

business_model.summary: Revenue is generated by growing, processing and selling almonds and their by-products (hulls/shells as stockfeed and biomass) from a mix of Company-owned/leased orchards and third-party (external grower) supply. Earnings are driven by three multiplicative levers: crop volume (own + external grower tonnes processed), the achieved almond price (a US-dollar global commodity price translated to AUD, with premiums captured through sales/marketing execution), and per-kg production/processing cost. A growing value-add segment (paste, blanched, roasted, sliced/diced almonds sold into beverage, bakery, confectionery, snacking and dairy/ice-cream customer categories) provides an incremental, higher-margin, more diversified revenue stream on top of bulk kernel and in-shell sales.

revenue_streams.name: External grower processing & associated sales/distribution margin
Value-added almond products (Allinga Farms: paste, roasted, sliced, diced)
By-products (hulls, shells, biomass/stockfeed, water trading gains)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - global almond traders, food & beverage manufacturers, and wholesalers/re-packers; no meaningful direct-to-consumer sales
business_model.geographic_mix: Almond price is a global USD-denominated commodity price; export destinations concentrated in China (~60-65% of sales, up ~25% YoY in FY2025), Türkiye, India, UAE, UK, Thailand, Denmark, Spain, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia. All production/growing assets are domestic (VIC, SA, NSW, Australia).

main_competitors: Olam Orchards Australia (largest Australian grower, ~12,000ha, owns the largest processing plant in the Southern Hemisphere near Mildura)
Stahmann Farms Enterprises (nut processor, diversifying into pecans)
Webster Limited (diversified agri producer with walnut and almond orchards)
Californian almond growers/processors (Blue Diamond Growers, Wonderful, Treehouse California Almonds) who supply ~75-80% of global almond volume
Numerous smaller independent Australian almond growers
competitive_position.market_position: Second-largest almond grower/processor in Australia (behind Olam Orchards) and third-largest almond grower globally; Australia is the world's second-largest almond producing country after the US (California), giving Select Harvests scale advantages versus other non-US growers but leaving it a price-taker versus the dominant Californian supply base.

moat_factors.description: Owns/leases orchards, runs its own large-scale processing facility (Carina West, 50,000MT capacity after 'Project Optimus' expansion) and its own sales/marketing function, capturing margin across horticulture, processing and marketing rather than being a pure grower or pure processor.

Large single-site processing facility with expanding capacity (added 20,000MT of capacity at low incremental capital cost) supports lower per-kg processing costs and the ability to service external growers, which is itself a growth and margin lever.
Australia has a more favourable tariff position than the US into key markets (notably China) amid US-China trade tensions, giving Australian-origin almonds a relative pricing/access advantage.
Traceable-to-orchard almond kernels, food-safety track record (customer complaints down 27% in FY2025) and the Allinga Farms value-add brand support premium positioning with manufacturing customers.
Multi-year lead time to establish bearing orchards and capital intensity of processing infrastructure create a moderate barrier to new large-scale entrants.

weaknesses: Price-taker in a global commodity market dominated by Californian supply (~75-80% of world production); Select Harvests has limited ability to influence the global almond price
High customer/geographic concentration in China (~60-65% of export sales), exposing the company to Chinese demand cycles, currency and geopolitical/trade-policy risk

Earnings and cash flow are structurally volatile due to weather-driven crop variability (FY2025 crop down 15.7% YoY) and IAS 41 biological asset fair-value accounting, which introduces non-cash valuation swings tied to yield and price assumptions
History of weak balance sheet/earnings (near-loss in FY2023, requiring an $80m capital raise in 2024) before the recent turnaround, reflecting limited resilience through prior down-cycles
Reliant on external inputs it does not control (water, bees, fertiliser, energy) that are subject to independent supply/cost shocks

growth_drivers: 2030 strategic targets: ~65,000MT of production/processing capacity and A$700m of revenue, roughly doubling the current ~45,000MT/ ~A$400m base
'Project Optimus' processing capacity expansion at Carina West to 50,000MT (with further debottlenecking toward 65,000MT) achieved at low incremental capital cost
External grower volume growth - targeting 20,000+MT annually (15,400MT already contracted for the 2026 crop), monetising spare processing capacity

Value-added product growth (Allinga Farms paste, roasted, sliced/diced) into beverage (almond milk), bakery, confectionery and snacking end-markets, with paste sales +20.7% in FY2025 and major contracts renewed
New in-line kernel recovery process (first of its kind in Australia) expected to lift yields by ~3% from the 2026 season

Structural supply tailwind: US/Californian bearing acreage has peaked and is now declining (first decline since 1995) with low replanting rates and water/cost constraints, supporting a firmer multi-year global almond price
Global demand growth for tree nuts/plant-based protein and healthy snacking, with industry forecasts of 5-7% CAGR in world almond demand
Horticultural and cost efficiency programs (new tree shakers, drainage/replant investment, ~A$10m of identified cost savings over two years) to improve yield and reduce per-kg costs
Balance sheet deleveraging (gearing down from 34.0% to 15.1% in FY2025) creating capacity for further growth capex or capital returns
Capital management: FY2025/26 on-market share buy-back (up to 10% of issued capital) and reinstated interim dividend signal confidence and support per-share value

business.description: Global USD almond pricing is the single largest driver of profitability and is set by Californian supply/demand dynamics outside the Company's control; FY2025 saw a sharp price swing on a surprise USDA California crop estimate before recovering.

Weather (frost, excess rain, drought) directly affects tonnage and quality; FY2025 crop fell 15.7% YoY and NSW orchards remain in recovery from prior wet seasons; a wet FY2026 harvest caused ~A$6.9m of one-off costs.

China represents roughly 60-65% of export sales; any slowdown in Chinese demand, change in trade policy, or renewed US-China tariff dynamics affecting relative competitiveness could materially impact sales and pricing.
Varroa mite spread, climatic factors and border movement restrictions have made bee availability for pollination increasingly problematic industry-wide.

The Carina West Processing Facility is a single-site, mission-critical asset; a catastrophic event (fire, flood, major equipment failure) could significantly disrupt operations and financial performance.

CEO David Surveyor, credited with the FY23-FY25 turnaround, resigned in mid-2026; incoming CEO Kristina Hermanson started 3 August 2026, creating near-term execution/continuity risk during a period of ambitious 2030 growth targets.

financial.description: Almond sales are transacted in USD while costs are largely AUD; AUD/USD movements affect reported profitability, partially managed via a Treasury and Risk Management Policy but not fully hedged.

IAS 41 fair-value accounting for orchards/growing crop introduces non-cash valuation volatility into the income statement tied to yield and price assumptions, complicating period-on-period earnings comparability.

Net debt is highly seasonal, rising materially during the growing/harvest season (H1 FY2026 net debt of ~A$183m versus FY2025 year-end net debt of A$79m) before being repaid as the crop is sold; a poor crop or price outcome could pressure covenants.
Water, bee hire, fertiliser, power and labour costs have risen; H1 FY2026 absorbed ~A$18m of inflationary cost increases only partly offset by identified savings.

regulatory.description: Murray-Darling Basin water entitlement policy, including government water buyback programs, can reduce available irrigation water and raise water prices, directly impacting orchard operating costs and viability.

Operations require ongoing environmental licences/permits (water usage, air quality, noise, biomass/compost operations); forthcoming mandatory AASB S2 climate disclosure requirements will increase compliance costs, though the Company reports no breaches to date.

US-China tariff dynamics currently advantage Australian almond exports relative to US supply, but any change in bilateral trade arrangements involving Australia or China could remove this relative advantage.

macro.description: The business is fundamentally exposed to the multi-year almond planting/bearing cycle in California (which supplies ~75-80% of global volume); a rebound in US supply or acreage could pressure prices industry-wide.

Seasonal working-capital debt funding (crop growing/harvest financed by drawn debt facilities) makes interest expense sensitive to interest rate movements, though refinancing in FY2025 secured improved terms across 3- and 5-year facilities.

The business is inherently cyclical, tied to weather, biological crop cycles and a global commodity price, producing lumpy year-to-year earnings (e.g., near break-even NPAT in FY2024 vs. $31.8m in FY2025).

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global almond demand is forecast to grow at a 5-7% CAGR, driven by rising demand for healthy/plant-based snacking and protein, particularly from China, India and Türkiye. Supply-side, Californian bearing acreage has peaked and is now declining for the first time since 1995 due to water constraints, rising input costs and low replanting rates, which industry commentary expects to keep global almond prices structurally firmer over the medium term.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - agricultural production is a biological, weather-dependent business subject to multi-year crop and pricing cycles; Select Harvests experienced a near break-even year in FY2023/24 followed by a sharp profit recovery in FY2025-26 driven mainly by price, illustrating high earnings cyclicality.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - seasonal working-capital debt is used to fund the growing/harvest cycle; net debt swings materially within the fiscal year (peaking mid-cycle, e.g. ~A$183m at H1 FY2026 vs A$79m at FY2025 year-end), making interest costs sensitive to base rate levels.
key_input_costs: Irrigation water (Murray-Darling entitlements and temporary/spot water)

recent_developments.event: Ongoing on-market share buy-back (up to 10% of issued capital, ~14.2m shares); as of 18 September 2026 the Company had repurchased a cumulative 2,462,374 shares, with the Board stating the current share price does not reflect intrinsic value.

New CEO Kristina Hermanson (25+ years' experience across agricultural processing, manufacturing, FMCG and institutional investment management) commenced 3 August 2026, succeeding David Surveyor who stepped down 31 July 2026 after leading the FY23-FY25 turnaround.

H1 FY2026 results: underlying NPAT of A$29.1m (+33% YoY), reported NPAT of A$26.6m; reinstated a fully franked interim dividend of 3.5 cents/share; announced 2030 strategic targets of 65,000MT production capacity and A$700m revenue; absorbed ~A$18m of input cost inflation and ~A$6.9m of one-off wet-harvest costs.
2026 crop guidance narrowed/raised to 28,800-29,600MT (+16-19% YoY) despite wet harvest conditions; ~77-91% of the 2026 crop hedged at approximately US$0.658-0.665/lb.

FY2025 Annual Report and Appendix 4E released: revenue from continuing operations up 35.3% to A$398.3m; NPAT of A$31.8m (vs A$0.9m restated FY2024), an increase of A$30.9m; EBITDA of A$82.4m; net debt reduced 51.3% to A$79.1m and gearing fell to 15.1% from 34.0%; almond price of A$10.18/kg (+32.4%) on a smaller 24,903MT crop (down 15.7%); no dividend declared for FY2025.
Refinanced debt facilities, securing A$240m in new funding across 3- and 5-year terms with improved pricing and an additional banking partner.
Completed rebalancing of the Company's water portfolio to better align water and farm locations, generating a A$5.8m one-off gain.

items.notes: Management guided to a substantial increase in both underlying and reported NPAT for FY2026, driven by second-half contribution from external grower processing, wholesale sales and value-added margins.
Represents a 16-19% increase versus the FY2025 crop of 24,903MT, narrowed/raised despite wet weather during harvest.

items.target: ~77-91% of 2026 crop hedged at approximately US$0.658-0.665/lb
items.notes: Provides visibility on a large majority of 2026 crop pricing; balance remains exposed to spot almond price movements.
Key lever to monetise expanded 50,000MT (moving toward 65,000MT) processing capacity.
Roughly a 45-50% increase versus current ~45,000MT combined own-crop plus external-grower processing base.
Implies roughly doubling FY2025 revenue of A$398.3m; management noted the Company has delivered comparable growth over the prior three years.
Aimed at offsetting inflationary pressure on water, fertiliser, power and labour costs.

items.vs_prior: raised (reinstated after no dividend in FY2024/FY2025)
items.notes: Marks return to capital distributions alongside the announced buy-back.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (outgoing CEO David Surveyor and CFO Liam Nolan, alongside the Board) expressed confidence that the macro environment for almonds remains positive, citing peaking/declining Californian bearing acreage, low replanting rates, water and cost constraints in California, and rising global demand (5-7% CAGR) from China, India and Türkiye. The Board set ambitious 2030 targets (65,000MT capacity, A$700m revenue) reflecting confidence the recent growth trajectory (FY23 near-loss to FY25 NPAT of A$31.8m, H1 FY26 underlying NPAT +33%) can continue. The Board also stated it believes the current share price does not reflect intrinsic value, underpinning the 10% buy-back.

bull_case: Structural almond supply tailwind: Californian bearing acreage has peaked and is declining for the first time since 1995, with low replanting and water/cost constraints, supporting a firmer multi-year global almond price backdrop

Company-specific turnaround momentum: NPAT rebuilt from near break-even (FY2023/24) to A$31.8m in FY2025 and +33% underlying NPAT growth in H1 FY2026, alongside gearing more than halved (34.0% to 15.1%) and a return to dividends/buy-backs

Multiple embedded growth levers largely self-funded: processing capacity expansion (Carina West to 50,000MT, targeting 65,000MT), external grower volume growth, and expanding value-added product sales, underpinning the Board's 2030 target of A$700m revenue

Demand-side tailwinds from rising global consumption of tree nuts/plant-based protein, with China, India and Türkiye demand described as strong, and Australia's tariff position in China currently more favourable than the US's
Management/Board signaling confidence via a 10% on-market buy-back and reinstated fully franked dividend, citing a belief the share price undervalues intrinsic value
bear_case: Fundamentally a price-taking commodity agribusiness: profitability is dominated by the globally-set USD almond price (set largely by Californian supply/demand), which the Company cannot control and which showed material volatility even within FY2025 alone

High concentration risk in China (~60-65% of export sales), leaving the Company exposed to Chinese demand shifts, currency movements and any change in relative US-China-Australia trade/tariff dynamics

Weather and biological risk create persistent earnings volatility: FY2025 crop volume fell 15.7% YoY, NSW orchards remain in multi-year recovery from prior wet seasons, and a wet FY2026 harvest already added ~A$6.9m of one-off costs

CEO transition risk at a pivotal moment, with the executive who led the FY23-25 turnaround departing just as the Company sets ambitious, capital-intensive 2030 growth targets (65,000MT capacity, A$700m revenue)

Rising uncontrollable input costs (water, bees, fertiliser, energy, labour) — H1 FY2026 alone absorbed ~A$18m of inflationary pressure — combined with seasonal working-capital debt swings that could strain the balance sheet in a weaker crop or price year
